patient.name: Tomás Ribeiro
patient.complaint: Three weeks of dry cough, fever and worsening breathlessness on exertion
background: Has sex with men; last HIV test 5 years ago
'Flu with a rash' that he ignored about 3 years ago
Barista in Vauxhall, no regular medication

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely causative organism?': a flu-like illness with rash and mouth ulcers after exposure (acute HIV), or an opportunistic infection that fits the CD4 count (PCP, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus, CMV).

points: Tomás, 34: **dry cough** and breathlessness for 3 weeks.
Breathless walking to the bus stop; fine at rest.

steps.lead: Tomás has the general features of untreated HIV: weight loss, fever, night sweats and a **non-productive cough**. His ignored 'flu with a rash' fits past **acute HIV**.
Tomás's risk is **unprotected sex**; injecting drugs and blood exposure are the other routes.

points: White plaques on his palate that scrape off: **oral candida**.
White corrugated patches on the sides of his tongue: **oral hairy leucoplakia**.
Small rubbery nodes in neck and axillae.

steps.q: Dry cough, exertional desaturation, clear chest, oral thrush. Which infection is most likely?
steps.r: **Desaturation on exertion** with a dry cough and a nearly clear chest in suspected HIV is classic **PCP**.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral perihilar interstitial shadowing, typical of Pneumocystis pneumonia.

steps.text: PCP can look near-normal early; perihilar haze is the classic pattern.

steps.lead: Tomás's PCP and thrush point to HIV destroying his **CD4 T-cells**, so his immunity is failing.
PCP is an **AIDS-defining illness**, so Tomás has advanced HIV whatever his CD4 count turns out to be.

steps.title: Opportunistic infections by CD4 count
head: CD4 (cells/mm³)
Think of
Clue
rows: Floaters, 'pizza pie' retina; headache, India ink

steps.lead: Tomás also needs checks for HIV-linked cancers: **Kaposi's sarcoma**, lymphomas, anal cancer.

steps.text: PCP is easy to miss: the chest may be **clear** and the CXR near-normal. The clue is **desaturation on exercise** in someone at risk.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' with the 4th generation antigen/antibody test as the answer, plus timing questions (window period, test at 4 weeks) and CD4 count or viral load for staging and monitoring.

steps.q: Which test diagnoses HIV in Tomás?
steps.r: The **4th generation antigen/antibody combined test** is the gold standard. CD4 and viral load stage and monitor.

steps.lead: Tomás's 4th generation test is reactive and a **confirmatory assay** is sent. His exposure was long ago, well past seroconversion.

steps.title: Tomás's results
steps.text: Advanced HIV with PCP: low CD4, high viral load, raised LDH, hypoxia.

visual.title: CD4 count
visual.label: Tomás 80
visual.caption: Below 200 defines AIDS and puts him at risk of PCP and toxoplasmosis.

steps.lead: Tomás's **CD4 count** stages him; his **viral load** shows activity and will track treatment. Hepatitis, TB, FBC and U&E screens are baseline.
Tomás has had some loose stools: as he is immunocompromised, he needs **stool microbiology** (cryptosporidium, C. difficile).
Tomás's partner had sex with him 2 weeks ago. NICE: offer testing to anyone at risk, and test asymptomatic contacts at **4 weeks** after exposure.

visual.title: Days since exposure: when will the test turn positive?
visual.label: Partner 14 days
visual.caption: A negative test now would be falsely reassuring: retest at 4 weeks, and POC tests need 90 days to exclude.

steps.text: PCP, TB, oral candida, shingles in the young and lymphoma are **indicator conditions**: always offer an HIV test.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' for an opportunistic infection (co-trimoxazole for PCP, amphotericin B plus flucytosine for cryptococcus, sulfadiazine plus pyrimethamine for toxoplasmosis, IV ganciclovir for CMV), cART for everyone regardless of CD4, prophylaxis below 200 and pregnancy questions.

steps.q: Tomás has PCP with PaO2 8.9 kPa. Which treatment?
steps.r: PCP: **co-trimoxazole**. Amphotericin plus flucytosine is cryptococcus, ganciclovir is CMV, sulfadiazine plus pyrimethamine is toxoplasmosis.

steps.lead: Breathless with a CD4 of 80: Tomás's **PCP** gets **co-trimoxazole** (with steroids as he is hypoxic, per BHIVA), watching for rash and cytopenias.

visual.title: Tomás's exertional saturations on treatment
visual.caption: Improving oxygenation; cART can be started within 2 weeks of PCP treatment.

steps.lead: Tomás starts **cART** under the HIV team: 2 **NRTIs** plus an **integrase inhibitor** such as dolutegravir. Everyone is treated, whatever the CD4.

steps.title: Typical first regimen
nodes: Or NRTI backbone + boosted protease inhibitor

steps.lead: With CD4 of 80, Tomás takes **co-trimoxazole prophylaxis**, gets non-live vaccines, safe sex advice and partner testing. His status stays **confidential**.

visual.title: Response to cART
visual.caption: Viral load undetectable by 6 months; prophylaxis can stop once CD4 stays above 200.

steps.lead: If Tomás's viral load stops falling, check **adherence** before anything else.
Not Tomás, but the exam loves pregnancy: **triple therapy** throughout, and a high viral load near delivery means **caesarean section**.

steps.text: Tomás's family visit. HIV status has **extra confidentiality protection**: do not tell relatives, even a doctor relative, without his consent.

steps.lead: Tomás's care follows **BHIVA/NICE** testing and treatment guidance; his partner may use the national **PEP** guideline in future exposures.

science.exam: Expect applied science: HIV as a retrovirus using reverse transcriptase to infect CD4 cells, the target of each drug class, why IRIS happens after starting cART, and HHV-8 in Kaposi's sarcoma.

points: Tomás asks how the virus 'ate' his immune system.
You sketch the HIV life cycle and where each tablet works.

steps.lead: HIV binds Tomás's **CD4+ T-helper cells**, copies its RNA into DNA with **reverse transcriptase** and integrates; CD4 cells die over years.

steps.title: HIV life cycle and drug targets
nodes: Integrase inserts DNA into host genome (integrase inhibitors)
Protease cuts proteins to mature virions (protease inhibitors)

steps.lead: Tomás's tenofovir and emtricitabine block **reverse transcriptase**; dolutegravir blocks **integrase**.

steps.r: Dolutegravir is an **integrase inhibitor**: it stops viral DNA being inserted into the host genome.

points: Week 3 of cART: new fever and swollen, painful neck nodes.
Lymph node aspirate: acid-fast bacilli; TB was there all along.
His CD4 is rising and viral load falling.

steps.lead: Tomás's recovering immune system is now attacking hidden TB: **IRIS**, a paradoxical worsening as immunity returns.
If Tomás developed purple skin lesions, **HHV-8** driving endothelial spindle cells (Kaposi's sarcoma) would be the cause.

steps.text: Thresholds to learn: **PCP <200**, **toxoplasmosis <100**, **CMV <50**. The lower the CD4, the stranger the infection.

mcq.q: Which CD4 count defines AIDS (without an AIDS-defining illness)?
mcq.r: CD4 below 200 cells/mm³ or an AIDS-defining illness.

mcq.q: Below which CD4 count is CMV retinitis typical?
mcq.r: CMV retinitis and cryptococcal meningitis typically occur below 50.
Human herpesvirus 8 drives endothelial spindle cell proliferation.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for HIV?
What is the window period of a point-of-care HIV antibody test?
mcq.r: POC tests need 90 days after exposure to exclude infection.

mcq.q: Which test monitors response to antiretroviral therapy?
mcq.r: Viral load shows disease activity; the goal is undetectable.

mcq.q: When should antiretroviral therapy be started?
mcq.r: All HIV-positive people are offered cART regardless of CD4 count.

mcq.q: What is the induction treatment for cryptococcal meningitis?
What must be done before starting PEP?
o: Viral load of the exposed person
mcq.r: An HIV test, to confirm the person is not already positive.

mcq.q: Which enzyme converts HIV RNA into DNA?
mcq.r: Reverse transcriptase; the target of NRTIs and NNRTIs.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a 'glandular fever' picture after a sexual exposure, with mucosal ulcers, is acute HIV until tested.

points.p: Flu-like illness with fever
points.why: Often missed as a simple viral illness.

points.p: Maculopapular rash on the upper body
points.why: A rash without amoxicillin in a glandular-fever picture.

points.p: Mucosal ulcers and lymphadenopathy
2 to 6 weeks after exposure, before or around seroconversion

prompts.q: What features suggest chronic or advanced HIV?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: weight loss, sweats and an odd infection in a young adult need an HIV test.

points.p: Often asymptomatic with gradual CD4 decline
points.why: Years can pass with no symptoms.

points.p: Weight loss, fatigue, fever, night sweats
Recurrent or opportunistic infections
points.why: Oral thrush in a non-immunosuppressed adult is a clue.

points.p: Oral hairy leucoplakia and lymphadenopathy
points.why: EBV-related white tongue patches that do not scrape off.

prompts.q: Which opportunistic infections appear at which CD4 counts?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the CD4 in the stem tells you which infection to pick.

points.p: Below 200: PCP, oesophageal candidiasis, cryptosporidiosis
Below 100: toxoplasmosis
Below 50: CMV retinitis and cryptococcal meningitis
points.why: The lowest counts give the rarest infections.

points.p: AIDS = CD4 below 200 or an AIDS-defining illness

prompts.q: What are the cancers and other complications linked to HIV?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: purple lesions in HIV = Kaposi's; nephrotic syndrome = HIVAN.

points.p: Kaposi's sarcoma (HHV-8)
points.why: Purple skin, palate or visceral lesions.

points.p: Lymphomas: primary CNS lymphoma, Hodgkin's, Burkitt's
Anal, liver and lung cancer
HIVAN: collapsing FSGS with nephrotic syndrome
PML

prompts.q: How is HIV diagnosed, and what about timing after an exposure?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a negative test too soon is falsely reassuring.

points.p: Gold standard: 4th generation antigen/antibody combined test
points.why: Detects p24 antigen as well as antibody.

points.p: Confirm with repeat or confirmatory assay
points.why: Never diagnose on one reactive result.

points.p: Seroconversion 3–12 weeks after exposure
Asymptomatic: test 4 weeks after exposure
points.why: Repeat later if the first test was early.

points.p: Point-of-care test: 90-day window period

prompts.q: Which tests stage and monitor HIV, and who should be offered testing?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: CD4 = immune status; viral load = disease activity.

points.p: CD4 count: immune status and AIDS diagnosis
Viral load (HIV RNA PCR): disease activity and treatment response
Baseline hepatitis and TB screens, FBC, U&E
Offer testing to high-prevalence groups and everyone at antenatal booking

prompts.q: What is the treatment for HIV and the long-term plan?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: CD4 count never delays cART.

points.p: cART for all, regardless of CD4 count, including pregnancy
2 NRTIs plus an integrase inhibitor (dolutegravir) or protease inhibitor
Co-trimoxazole PCP prophylaxis if CD4 below 200
Non-live vaccines, safe sex, partner testing, confidentiality
points.why: Live vaccines are avoided when CD4 is low.

points.p: PEP after significant exposure, after an HIV test

prompts.q: How are the main opportunistic infections treated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match each organism to its drug.

points.p: PCP: co-trimoxazole
Toxoplasmosis: sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine
Cryptococcal meningitis: IV amphotericin B plus flucytosine
CMV retinitis: IV ganciclovir

prompts.q: How is HIV managed in pregnancy?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: viral load near delivery decides the mode of delivery.

points.p: Triple therapy: 2 NRTIs plus integrase inhibitor or protease inhibitor
High maternal viral load: caesarean section
Test everyone at antenatal booking
points.why: Undiagnosed HIV is the main transmission risk.

prompts.q: How does HIV cause immune failure, and how do the drug classes work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the drug class to its step in the life cycle.

points.p: Retrovirus infects and destroys CD4+ T-helper cells
Reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA to DNA for integration
NRTIs and NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcriptase
Protease inhibitors block viral protein maturation
Integrase inhibitors stop viral DNA entering the host genome

prompts.q: What is IRIS and why does Kaposi's sarcoma occur?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: getting worse after starting cART is IRIS, not drug failure.

points.p: IRIS: cART in a severely immunosuppressed patient
Recovering immune system over-reacts to hidden or partly treated infection such as TB
Kaposi's: HHV-8 drives endothelial spindle cell proliferation with immunosuppression

glossary.HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus: a retrovirus that destroys CD4 T-cells.
glossary.AIDS: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome: CD4 below 200 or an AIDS-defining illness.
glossary.CD4 count: Number of CD4 helper T-cells in blood; shows immune status in HIV.
glossary.CD4: Surface marker on T-helper cells that HIV uses to enter cells.
glossary.Viral load: Amount of HIV RNA in blood, measured by PCR, showing disease activity.
glossary.Seroconversion: When antibodies to HIV first appear, 3 to 12 weeks after infection.
glossary.Window period: Time after infection when a test can still be negative.
glossary.4th generation: HIV test detecting both p24 antigen and antibody, so it turns positive earlier.
glossary.p24 antigen: An HIV core protein detected early in infection by 4th generation tests.
glossary.Point-of-care test: Rapid finger-prick antibody test giving a result in minutes; 90-day window period.
glossary.cART: Combination antiretroviral therapy: usually three drugs from at least two classes.
glossary.NRTI: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, e.g. tenofovir, emtricitabine, abacavir, lamivudine.
glossary.Integrase inhibitor: Drug such as dolutegravir that stops viral DNA joining the host genome.
glossary.Protease inhibitor: Drug such as atazanavir that stops viral proteins maturing.
glossary.Dolutegravir: An integrase inhibitor used in first-line HIV regimens.
glossary.Reverse transcriptase: Viral enzyme that copies RNA into DNA.
glossary.Retrovirus: RNA virus that copies itself into DNA and inserts it into the host genome.
glossary.PCP: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: dry cough and exertional desaturation when CD4 is below 200.
glossary.Pneumocystis jirovecii: Fungus causing pneumonia in people with CD4 below 200.
glossary.Co-trimoxazole: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole; treats and prevents PCP.
glossary.Toxoplasmosis: Toxoplasma gondii infection causing ring-enhancing brain lesions when CD4 is below 100.
glossary.Cryptococcal meningitis: Fungal meningitis from Cryptococcus neoformans, usually when CD4 is below 50.
glossary.India ink: CSF stain that shows the capsule of Cryptococcus.
glossary.CMV retinitis: Cytomegalovirus infection of the retina causing floaters and visual loss when CD4 is below 50.
glossary.Ganciclovir: Antiviral used intravenously for CMV retinitis.
glossary.Amphotericin B: Antifungal used with flucytosine to induce treatment of cryptococcal meningitis.
glossary.Flucytosine: Antifungal combined with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis.
glossary.Sulfadiazine: Sulfonamide used with pyrimethamine to treat toxoplasmosis.
glossary.Pyrimethamine: Antiparasitic used with sulfadiazine for toxoplasmosis.
glossary.Kaposi's sarcoma: HHV-8 driven tumour of endothelial cells causing purple skin and mucosal lesions.
glossary.HHV-8: Human herpesvirus 8, the cause of Kaposi's sarcoma.
glossary.Oral hairy leucoplakia: White corrugated patches on the side of the tongue from EBV, a sign of immunosuppression.
glossary.Oral candida: Thrush: white plaques in the mouth that scrape off.
glossary.Oesophageal candidiasis: Candida infection of the oesophagus causing painful swallowing; AIDS-defining.
glossary.Cryptosporidiosis: Parasitic infection causing chronic watery diarrhoea in advanced HIV.
glossary.PML: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: JC virus brain demyelination in severe immunosuppression.
glossary.Primary CNS lymphoma: EBV-driven brain lymphoma in advanced HIV, usually a single lesion.
glossary.HIVAN: HIV-associated nephropathy: collapsing FSGS causing nephrotic syndrome.
glossary.FSGS: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, a cause of nephrotic syndrome.
glossary.IRIS: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome: worsening of a hidden infection as immunity recovers on cART.
glossary.PEP: Post-exposure prophylaxis: 28 days of antiretrovirals after a significant exposure.
glossary.AIDS-defining illness: An infection or cancer, such as PCP or Kaposi's, that diagnoses AIDS whatever the CD4.
glossary.Indicator condition: An illness that should prompt an HIV test, such as TB, shingles in the young or lymphoma.
glossary.Slamming: Injecting recreational drugs during sex; a risk for HIV through shared needles.
glossary.GUM: Genitourinary medicine: the specialty managing sexual health and HIV.
glossary.BHIVA: British HIV Association, which publishes UK HIV guidelines.
glossary.Stevens-Johnson syndrome: Severe blistering drug reaction of skin and mucosa, a risk with co-trimoxazole.
glossary.Agranulocytosis: Severe loss of neutrophils, a side effect of co-trimoxazole.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man has a 5 day history of fever, sore throat and a rash. He had unprotected sex with a new male partner 3 weeks ago. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. There is a maculopapular rash over his chest and back, shallow ulcers in his mouth and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. He has not taken any antibiotics.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: a glandular-fever picture, so look for the exposure.

clues: unprotected sex with a new male partner 3 weeks ago
maculopapular rash over his chest and back
steps.x: Exposure 3 weeks ago; upper body rash; mucosal ulcers; no amoxicillin to explain a rash.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Flu-like illness, rash and mucosal ulcers weeks after exposure = **acute HIV infection**.

elim: CMV gives a mononucleosis picture but not mucosal ulcers after an exposure.
Glandular fever rash usually follows amoxicillin; ulcers are not typical.
Secondary syphilis comes 6 weeks or more after a chancre, with palm and sole rash.
Strep tonsillitis has exudate, no rash or ulcers here.

steps.x: **A. Acute HIV infection.** Rule: flu-like illness + rash + mouth ulcers after exposure = test for HIV.

technique.stem: A 26 year old woman attends a sexual health clinic. She had unprotected sex with a man of unknown HIV status 12 days ago. She is well with no symptoms. She is not eligible for PEP as it is more than 72 hours since exposure. She asks for a test to rule out HIV.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: HIV antigen/antibody test 4 weeks after exposure
No test as she is asymptomatic
Point-of-care antibody test now with no repeat

steps.x: Investigation: and the timing matters.
Asymptomatic, exposure under 4 weeks ago.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Asymptomatic contacts are tested at **4 weeks** with the 4th generation test; earlier tests can be falsely negative.

elim: CD4 does not diagnose HIV.
Viral load is not the screening test.
NICE offers testing to anyone at risk, even if asymptomatic.
POC tests have a 90-day window, so a negative at 12 days excludes nothing.

steps.x: **B. 4th gen test at 4 weeks.** Rule: test at 4 weeks; POC window is 90 days.

technique.stem: A 39 year old man with newly diagnosed HIV has 2 weeks of dry cough and breathlessness on exertion. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 120/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% at rest, falling to 87% on walking. His CD4 count is 60 cells/mm³.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management: name the infection first.
Exertional desaturation, dry cough, CD4 below 200.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: This is **PCP**: treat with **co-trimoxazole**.

elim: Amphotericin plus flucytosine is for cryptococcal meningitis.
Ganciclovir is for CMV retinitis.
RIPE is for TB, which gives productive cough and cavities.
Sulfadiazine plus pyrimethamine is for toxoplasmosis.

steps.x: **A. Co-trimoxazole.** Rule: breathless + low CD4 = PCP = co-trimoxazole.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman with HIV starts a regimen of tenofovir, emtricitabine and dolutegravir. She asks how the third drug works.
technique.q: Which is the mechanism of action of dolutegravir?
o: Prevents integration of viral DNA into the host genome
Prevents viral fusion with the cell membrane

steps.x: Drug mechanism: recognise the class from the name.
Two NRTIs plus a '-tegravir' drug.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: '-tegravir' = **integrase inhibitor**: stops viral DNA integrating into the host genome.

elim: CCR5 blockade is maraviroc.
Protease inhibitors (atazanavir) block maturation.
Tenofovir and emtricitabine are the reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
Fusion inhibitors (enfuvirtide) are rarely used.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: -tegravir = integrase; -navir = protease; tenofovir/emtricitabine = NRTI.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man who injects heroin and shares needles has lost 8 kg over 4 months and has night sweats. He has had shingles twice in the past year. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. There are white plaques on his palate that scrape off and generalised lymphadenopathy.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

steps.x: Underlying diagnosis: what ties these together?

clues: white plaques on his palate that scrape off
steps.x: Needle sharing, weight loss, recurrent shingles, oral candida, nodes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Recurrent and opportunistic infections in an at-risk adult = **chronic HIV infection**.

elim: AML gives cytopenias and bleeding, not recurrent shingles and needle-sharing risk.
Diabetes can cause thrush but not weight loss with nodes and recurrent shingles here.
Hodgkin's gives nodes and sweats but does not explain the risk and the infections.
Sarcoidosis causes hilar nodes and skin or eye signs, not candida.

steps.x: **B. Chronic HIV infection.** Rule: oral thrush + recurrent shingles + risk = HIV test.

practice.e: Needle sharing with weight loss, recurrent shingles, oral candida and lymphadenopathy points to chronic HIV. A normal HbA1c makes diabetes unlikely.

practice.stem: A 42 year old man with HIV who stopped his antiretrovirals a year ago has 3 weeks of dry cough and breathlessness on exertion. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% at rest, falling to 85% on walking. His chest is clear. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral perihilar interstitial shadowing, typical of Pneumocystis pneumonia.

practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: Organism question: use the CD4 and the oxygen clue.
Untreated HIV, dry cough, exertional desaturation, clear chest, perihilar haze.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pneumocystis jirovecii**: the CD4 below 200 pneumonia.

elim: H. influenzae gives productive cough with focal signs.
TB gives productive cough, upper-zone cavities, haemoptysis.
S. aureus gives cavitating consolidation after flu.
Pneumococcus gives productive cough and lobar consolidation.

steps.x: **C. Pneumocystis jirovecii.** Rule: HIV + exertional desaturation + clear chest = PCP.

practice.e: Exertional desaturation with a dry cough, clear chest and perihilar shadowing at CD4 110 is PCP. Bacterial pneumonias give productive cough and focal consolidation.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman with untreated HIV has a 2 week history of worsening headache, fever and vomiting. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Neck stiffness is mild. CT head is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: Organism question: read the CSF.
Subacute meningitis, very low CD4, India ink positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: India ink capsules + CD4 below 50 = **Cryptococcus neoformans**.

elim: Aspergillus causes lung disease in neutropenia.
Candida causes oral or oesophageal disease.
Listeria meningitis is acute; India ink would be negative.
Toxoplasma gives ring-enhancing lesions on CT, not meningitis.

steps.x: **C. Cryptococcus neoformans.** Rule: HIV + subacute meningitis + India ink = cryptococcus.

practice.e: Subacute headache with raised opening pressure and India ink-positive yeasts at CD4 35 is cryptococcal meningitis. Toxoplasma causes focal ring-enhancing lesions.

practice.stem: A 40 year old man with HIV who does not take his treatment has a focal seizure and right arm weakness. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. His CD4 count is 70 cells/mm³. Contrast CT head shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: brain lesions in advanced HIV.
CD4 below 100; multiple ring-enhancing lesions.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions at CD4 below 100 = **cerebral toxoplasmosis**.

elim: Cryptococcus gives meningitis, not ring lesions.
Glioblastoma is usually a single mass in older adults.
Primary CNS lymphoma is usually a single lesion and EBV-positive.
PML gives non-enhancing white matter lesions.

steps.x: **E. Toxoplasmosis.** Rule: multiple ring-enhancing lesions + CD4 <100 = toxo.

practice.e: Multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions at CD4 70 is cerebral toxoplasmosis. Primary CNS lymphoma is usually solitary and PML does not enhance.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 90 cells/mm³ has several painless purple nodules on his legs and a purple plaque on his hard palate. They have slowly enlarged over 2 months. They do not blanch.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: skin lesion in HIV.

clues: purple plaque on his hard palate
steps.x: Low CD4; multiple purple skin and palate lesions.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Purple skin and palate lesions in HIV = **Kaposi's sarcoma** (HHV-8).

elim: Cherry angiomas are small bright red papules, not palatal plaques.
Dermatofibroma is a single firm brown nodule.
Melanoma is usually single and pigmented, not multiple with palatal lesions.
Pyogenic granuloma is a single bleeding red lump.

steps.x: **C. Kaposi's sarcoma.** Rule: HIV + purple skin or palate lesions = Kaposi's.

practice.e: Multiple purple nodules with a palatal plaque in advanced HIV is Kaposi's sarcoma, driven by HHV-8. Melanoma is usually solitary.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man with HIV who has never taken treatment has 1 week of floaters and blurred vision in his right eye. The eye is not painful or red. His CD4 count is 25 cells/mm³. Fundoscopy shows retinal haemorrhages with fluffy white exudates along the vessels.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: visual loss in advanced HIV.
Painless, CD4 below 50, haemorrhage and exudate retina.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CD4 below 50 + 'pizza pie' retina = **CMV retinitis**.

elim: Angle closure is painful and red with a fixed pupil.
Anterior uveitis is painful and red with photophobia.
CRVO occurs in older vascular patients; CD4 25 is the clue here.
He has no diabetes.

steps.x: **D. CMV retinitis.** Rule: HIV + CD4 <50 + floaters + haemorrhagic retinitis = CMV.

practice.e: Painless floaters with haemorrhages and exudates at CD4 25 is CMV retinitis, treated with IV ganciclovir. Uveitis and glaucoma are painful and red.

practice.stem: A 29 year old man has a 4 month history of weight loss and recurrent oral thrush. He has had several male sexual partners. He has never had an HIV test. He agrees to testing.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation for HIV.
Indicator condition, risk factor, never tested.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gold standard: **4th generation antigen/antibody combined test**, confirmed by repeat.

elim: CD4 stages immunity; it does not diagnose HIV.
Viral load monitors disease activity, not screening.
Biopsy is for lymphoma, not first.
Western blot is no longer the diagnostic test.

steps.x: **B. 4th generation Ag/Ab test.** Rule: diagnose with 4th gen; stage with CD4; monitor with viral load.

practice.e: HIV is diagnosed with a 4th generation antigen/antibody test and confirmed by repeat testing. CD4 count and viral load are for staging and monitoring.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman with HIV started tenofovir, emtricitabine and dolutegravir 3 months ago. She takes every dose. Her doctor wants to know whether the treatment is controlling the virus.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: Investigation that monitors treatment.
On cART, checking disease activity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Viral load (HIV RNA PCR)**: the goal is undetectable.

elim: CD4 shows immune recovery, not viral control.
CRP is a non-specific inflammation marker.
Antibodies stay positive for life.
p24 is part of the diagnostic test, not monitoring.

steps.x: **D. Viral load.** Rule: viral load monitors treatment; CD4 guides prophylaxis.

practice.e: Viral load (HIV RNA PCR) measures disease activity and response to cART; the target is undetectable. CD4 count reflects immune status.

practice.stem: A 27 year old man is diagnosed with HIV at a routine sexual health screen. He is well. His CD4 count is 650 cells/mm³ and his viral load is 35,000 copies/mL. He is keen to do whatever is best for his health and his partner.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Start cART only when CD4 falls below 350

steps.x: Management: does the CD4 count change the plan?
Asymptomatic, normal CD4.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: All HIV-positive patients get **cART regardless of CD4**.

elim: Waiting is no longer recommended.
CD4 thresholds for starting were abandoned.
Prophylaxis is only needed when CD4 is below 200.
Monotherapy breeds resistance.

steps.x: **D. Start cART now.** Rule: cART for all, whatever the CD4.

practice.e: All people with HIV are offered cART regardless of CD4 count, reducing illness and transmission. Co-trimoxazole is only needed below CD4 200.

practice.stem: A 41 year old woman is newly diagnosed with HIV. Her CD4 count is 150 cells/mm³. She is well with no symptoms of infection. She is starting combination antiretroviral therapy.
practice.q: Which additional drug is most appropriate?

steps.x: Additional drug: prophylaxis guided by CD4.
CD4 below 200, no active infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CD4 below 200 = **co-trimoxazole** PCP prophylaxis.

elim: Aciclovir is for herpes infections, not routine prophylaxis.
Azithromycin is MAC prophylaxis at much lower CD4, if at all.
Fluconazole treats candida, not routine prophylaxis.
Isoniazid is for latent TB, not shown here.

steps.x: **C. Co-trimoxazole.** Rule: CD4 <200 → co-trimoxazole prophylaxis.

practice.e: With a CD4 below 200 she should take co-trimoxazole to prevent PCP alongside cART. Azithromycin and fluconazole are not routine prophylaxis here.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman with HIV is 36 weeks pregnant. She has struggled to take her antiretroviral therapy regularly. Her viral load is 15,000 copies/mL and her CD4 count is 280 cells/mm³.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate mode of delivery?
o: Vaginal delivery after artificial rupture of membranes

steps.x: Mode of delivery: the viral load decides.
Poor adherence and high viral load near term.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: High maternal viral load = **caesarean section** to reduce transmission.

elim: Induction leads to vaginal delivery, which is unsafe with this viral load.
Instruments increase fetal exposure to maternal blood.
Vaginal delivery is only for a suppressed viral load.
Artificial rupture prolongs exposure to infected secretions.

steps.x: **A. Elective caesarean section.** Rule: high viral load at delivery = caesarean.

practice.e: A high maternal viral load near delivery means an elective caesarean section to cut transmission risk. Vaginal delivery is only planned when the viral load is suppressed.

practice.stem: A 37 year old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 30 cells/mm³ starts cART. Three weeks later he develops fever and painful, swollen cervical lymph nodes. Aspirate shows acid-fast bacilli. His viral load has fallen and his CD4 count has risen to 110 cells/mm³. He takes every dose.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his deterioration?
o: Recovering immune response to an existing infection

steps.x: Mechanism: getting worse while the numbers get better.
Very low CD4 at start; inflammation as immunity recovers; hidden TB.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IRIS**: the recovering immune system over-reacts to hidden TB.

elim: A drug reaction would not produce acid-fast bacilli in nodes.
Resistance would mean a rising viral load.
He has not been in hospital.
He has not had TB treatment, so there is no rifampicin failure.

steps.x: **D. Recovering immune response.** Rule: worse weeks after cART with rising CD4 = IRIS.

practice.e: IRIS happens when cART restores immunity in severe immunosuppression and the immune system attacks a hidden infection such as TB. Falling viral load rules out resistance.
